To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Twelve weeks of moderate intensity (73-82% of maximal HR) low cadence training (40 rpm) twice a week, in well-trained veteran cyclists, did not result in improvements of cycling performance, aerobic capacity or leg strength.

12 weeks of low cadance interval training (40 rpm) at moderate intensity (75–82% of heart rate maximum) twice a week in addition to usual training does not improve cycling capacity or performance in veteran cyclists, but that 12 weeks training at same intensity and duration at freely chosen cadance does improve performance.
low cadence training (40 rpm) at moderate intensity (75–80% HRmax) twice per week for 12 weeks does not improve aerobic power or cycling performance in well trained veteran cyclists.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of low cadences on performance and physiological adaptations in highly trained veteran male cyclists.
the question of whether low cadence interval training can be an effective method to increase cycling performance.
the effects of low cadences (40 rpm) during training at moderate intensity in veteran cyclists.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
adding 90 min of moderate training at freely chosen intensity and cadence to the normal training program is beneficial for performance and adaptations in highly trained veteran athletes.
low cadence interval training does not improve cycling endurance performance in well-trained cyclists.
a moderate intensity training program with low cadence (≤ 60 rpm) does not improve aerobic performance in highly trained veterans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
low cadence interval training (40 rpm) does not improve cycling endurance performance in highly trained veterans cyclists.
low cadence interval training does not improve cycling performances in well trained veteran cyclists.
training at low cadence does not improve performance in highly trained cyclists.
The main takeaway from our work is that
training at a freely chosen cadence may be more effective than low cadence training for performance and physiological improvement in veteran cyclists.
training at freely chosen pedaling cadence is more efficient than training with a prescribed pedaling cadence.
training at freely chosen intensity is beneficial for performance and aerobic adaptations, while low cadence interval training is not.
